files.Blockchain/Dev/deployment/KINTSUGI-DEV-S:
# Kintsugi — Platform K dev server, and the dev/demo split

**Ticket:** [KS-601](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-601) · **Status:** Stage A complete (this document). **Stage B — creating the VM — has NOT been run and needs Kam's explicit go on spend.**

Today Platform K has **one** VM, `secuura02-demo-vm`, and it is simultaneously the demo, the staging target and the only place integration work can be exercised. Kintsugi is the second box that ends that. This document is everything short of spending money.

---

## 1. Sizing — measured against what the demo VM actually does, not guessed

Read read-only from `secuura02-demo-vm` on 2026-08-17:

| | measured |
| -- | -- |
| Size today | `Standard_B2pls_v2` — 2 vCPU ARM64 (Neoverse-N1), 4 GiB |
| Containers running | **33** |
| Container memory in use | **1081 MiB** total |
| Host memory | 3899 MiB total, 2613 MiB used, **765 MiB swapped out** at idle |
| Load average | **0.06** (1 min) |
| Disk | 61 GiB, 37 GiB used (61%) |
| Docker images | 12.78 GB |
| Docker build cache | **16.79 GB** (13.54 GB reclaimable) |

**The finding that drives the sizing: this box is memory-bound, not CPU-bound.** It is swapping 765 MiB at idle while the CPU sits at 6% of one core — and it does **not** build images; images are built there only during a deploy. Kintsugi's whole purpose is to build and re-build continuously, which is the memory- and disk-hungry part. Sizing it like demo would reproduce demo's worst characteristic and add a new one.

Two corollaries: **more RAM matters, more vCPU mostly does not**, and **disk must grow** — build cache alone is already 16.79 GB on a machine that only builds occasionally.

## 2. Options — real Azure retail prices, AUD, `southeastasia`, fetched 2026-08-17

| | VM | vCPU / RAM | Disk | **AUD/month** |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| **A — like-for-like** | `Standard_B2pls_v2` | 2 / 4 GiB (burstable) | 64 GiB E6 | 44.82 + 6.96 + 3.80 = **$55.58** |
| **B — recommended** | `Standard_D2ps_v6` | 2 / 8 GiB (**non-burstable**) | 128 GiB E10 | 92.49 + 13.91 + 3.80 = **$110.20** |
| **C — headroom** | `Standard_B4ps_v2` | 4 / 16 GiB (burstable) | 128 GiB E10 | 179.87 + 13.91 + 3.80 = **$197.58** |

All prices are the published retail rate (Azure Retail Prices API, `currencyCode=AUD`), VM + managed disk + static public IP, 730 h/month. They are list prices, before any Founders Hub credit.

### Recommendation: **Option B**, and the reason is a $2.77 difference

The obvious pick looked like `Standard_B2ps_v2` — 2 vCPU / 8 GiB, burstable, **$89.72**/mo, so **$107.43** all-in. Pricing the non-burstable equivalent changed the answer: `Standard_D2ps_v6` is the same 2 vCPU / 8 GiB **without** CPU-credit throttling for **$92.49**/mo — **$2.77/month more**.

B-series machines run on CPU credits and throttle hard once the credits are spent. That is fine for a demo that idles at 6%. It is the wrong shape for a box whose job is compiling TypeScript and building 30 container images, where load arrives in long sustained bursts — exactly the pattern that exhausts credits. **Paying $2.77/month to remove that failure mode is not a close call.**

**Option A is a trap** and is listed only so the cheap option is on the record: demo already swaps at idle on that size *without* building anything.

**Option C buys build speed, nothing else.** For calibration: rebuilding two services (`auth` + `originate`) on the current 2-vCPU box took **~9 minutes** today. Four vCPUs would roughly halve that. If the team finds build latency painful in practice, C is the upgrade — and resizing an Azure VM later is a stop/resize/start, not a rebuild, so **starting at B and moving to C if needed costs nothing but a reboot.** That reversibility is why B is the right first commitment.

### 🔴 Before committing to any of these

Project records show the **Founders Hub credit expires 6 September 2026** — about three weeks out. Whichever option is chosen, the standing cost is what matters, not the credited cost. **This should be confirmed against the current subscription before the spend decision**, not taken from these notes. The subscription's consumption API returned no usage data to this credential, so I could not measure current burn to put alongside these figures.

---

## 3. Provisioning — written, reviewed, **not run**

Stage B. Every command below is inert until someone runs it deliberately.

```bash
# --- guardrail: never run any of this without confirming the tenant first ---
export AZURE_CONFIG_DIR="$PROJECT_DIR/4_Credentials/.azure"
az account show --query "{tenant:tenantId, sub:id}" -o tsv
#   MUST be efc17e5f-7637-4118-b92c-c5236d591cad / a0ee7d32-2e4a-47a0-9a49-9c001817a545

RG=secuura-demo-rg           # same RG as demo; separate VM, separate vnet
LOC=southeastasia
VM=secuura02-kintsugi-vm
SIZE=Standard_D2ps_v6        # Option B
KEY=3_Access_Keys/vm_secuura02_kintsugi   # generate first, gitignored, never committed

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f "$KEY" -N '' -C 'kintsugi-dev'

az vm create \
  --resource-group "$RG" --name "$VM" --location "$LOC" \
  --image Ubuntu2404 --size "$SIZE" \
  --admin-username secuura --ssh-key-values "${KEY}.pub" \
  --public-ip-sku Standard --public-ip-address-dns-name secuura02-kintsugi \
  --os-disk-size-gb 128 --storage-sku StandardSSD_LRS \
  --vnet-name secuura02-kintsugi-vnet --subnet default

# Ports: 22 from the office/dev IPs only, 80+443 for Caddy's ACME + the portals.
# Do NOT open 5432/6379/6432 — KS-614/F-4 bound those to loopback for a reason.
az vm open-port -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --port 80  --priority 1010
az vm open-port -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --port 443 --priority 1020

# Swap, as demo has (6 GiB). Docker. Then the stack.
ssh -i "$KEY" secuura@<ip> 'sudo fallocate -l 6G /swapfile && sudo chmod 600 /swapfile \
  && sudo mkswap /swapfile && sudo swapon /swapfile \
  && echo "/swapfile none swap sw 0 0" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab'
```

Stack bring-up follows `DEPLOYMENT-ARCHITECTURE.md` §Redeploy runbook. **Three traps that must be carried across, because each has already cost this project a session:**

1. **Never rsync `.env` / `.env.local`.** Kintsugi gets its **own** `.env`, authored on the box. Copying demo's is what caused the 2026-07-30→08-02 mock-anchoring incident.
2. **Never pass `--remove-orphans` to `docker compose up`.** It deletes `guardian` and `queue`, which sit behind the `phase2` profile.
3. **Migrations are baked into an image.** Rebuild the `migrations` service alongside the others and verify the schema changed directly — the runner prints `failed=0` even when it never saw the new file.

And one that is specific to a *dev* box: **a successful write probe against a real preview-testnet stack anchors on chain.** Kintsugi must get its own wallet (§4) before anyone exercises a write path, or it will race demo for the same UTxOs — the exact KS-535 failure.

## 4. Kintsugi's own preview wallet — procedure now, execution at Stage C

**KS-535 is absolute: Kintsugi must never share demo's `PLATFORM_WALLET_MNEMONIC`.** Two deployments on one wallet select the same UTxOs and race; the loser fails with `All inputs are spent`. That has already happened at scale — 295 local and 2 demo anchors.

Procedure:

1. Generate a **fresh** BIP-39 mnemonic on the Kintsugi box itself.
2. Fund from the Cardano preview faucet — <https://docs.cardano.org/cardano-testnets/tools/faucet>. Testnet ADA, no real money.
3. Store in Kintsugi's own gitignored `.env` and back up as a Key Vault secret alongside demo's (`secuura02-demo-kv/platform-wallet-mnemonic` is the existing pattern; use a distinct name).
4. On first boot, confirm the log line reads `cardanoMode: REAL (Blockfrost)` and the wallet address is **not** `addr_test1qrjjw7rr…` (demo's).

**Deliberately deferred to Stage C rather than done now.** The wallet cannot be funded or verified until the box exists, and creating a credential three weeks before it is used means three weeks of it sitting somewhere unverified. Generating it at first boot is both safer and simpler.

**Open question for the Stage B/C decision: does Kintsugi need its own Blockfrost project key?** Blockfrost meters by project, so sharing demo's key means dev traffic consumes demo's quota and the two become indistinguishable in Blockfrost's own usage view. A separate free-tier preview project is the clean answer and costs nothing — worth confirming before Stage C rather than discovering it as a rate-limit.

## 5. The promotion gate — the process half, which needs no server

This is the part of the split that can be adopted immediately and matters most.

**Today:** `develop` merges land, and the demo VM is redeployed to match. Demo is simultaneously the integration target, the staging environment, and the thing shown to people.

**After cutover:**

| | Kintsugi | `secuura02-demo-vm` |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Role | dev + integration | **demo + staging only** |
| Deploys | freely, from `develop`, by any agent or dev | **only on an explicit promote** |
| Who may trigger | anyone working the stack | **Kam + Peter + Stuart go-ahead, every promote** |
| Purpose | break things, exercise write paths, test migrations | be trustworthy when someone is watching |

**The rule, stated so it can be quoted:** *develop and test on Kintsugi; promote to the demo VM only on Kam, Peter and Stuart's go-ahead — every promote, not once.*

Two consequences worth naming now:

- **In-development work stops being deployed to demo.** The KS-584 P3 work is the immediate example: it goes onto Kintsugi, never onto demo mid-development.
- **A promote becomes a reviewable event**, which is what makes "the demo is trustworthy" a property rather than a hope.

## 6. DNS and TLS — plan only, no records created

**`kintsugi.secuura.net` is contested and must not be created yet.** Verified 2026-08-17: it does not resolve at all today, while `dev-ps.secuura.net` → `20.24.185.177` (the PS estate's .NET Identity stack) and `demo-pk.secuura.net` → the K demo VM. A separate environment-naming proposal maps the Kintsugi name onto the **PS** estate's dev host, while KS-601 defines Kintsugi as the **Platform K** dev server.

> **⚠ SUPERSEDED BY EVENTS — re-verified 2026-08-20 (session 53).** The record
> was created and the name now points at the Platform K box. Measured, not
> assumed:
>
> | name | resolves to | serves |
> | -- | -- | -- |
> | `kintsugi.secuura.net` | CNAME → `secuura02-kintsugi.southeastasia.cloudapp.azure.com` → `20.198.226.148` | HTTP 200 (K stack) |
> | `dev-ps.secuura.net` | `20.24.185.177` | PS estate — **unchanged, still PS** |
> | `demo-pk.secuura.net` | `secuura02-demo.southeastasia.cloudapp.azure.com` → `20.212.118.59` | K demo VM |
>
> A Let's Encrypt certificate `CN=kintsugi.secuura.net` was issued
> **2026-08-19 21:55:57 UTC** (expires 2026-11-17). So the paragraph below —
> *"settle the name before a record exists"* — has been overtaken: by its own
> terms, reassigning the name is now **a migration rather than a decision**.
> Raising it on KS-601 rather than silently rewriting the plan, because the
> naming question was Kam's to settle and the record was created without that
> being recorded anywhere.
>
> `20.24.185.177` above is **correct and current** — it is the PS dev host, not
> a stale Kintsugi address. Do not SSH to it expecting Kintsugi; the K dev box
> is `20.198.226.148`.

**Therefore:** stand the box up on its **Azure-assigned FQDN** (`secuura02-kintsugi.southeastasia.cloudapp.azure.com`). Caddy issues a Let's Encrypt certificate for that name automatically, exactly as demo does, so there is no TLS dependency on the pretty name at all. The friendly name is a CNAME added later, once Kam settles which box owns it.

**Settle the name before a record exists.** After a record is created and certificates are issued against it, changing owners becomes a migration rather than a decision.

---
